intro: When you search for a kitchen extension architect near me, you are likely planning to open up the back of your home and want a professional who understands how a new kitchen, dining and living space should work. You need someone local who can design a layout that suits how you cook and gather, and who can guide you through planning and building regulations.
need_heading: What people searching for a kitchen extension architect usually need
need_lead: Most people want a practical, light-filled kitchen extension that feels part of the home, not just an add-on.
needs: You want an open-plan kitchen that flows into a dining and living area without awkward corners or dark spots.
You need help working out where the sink, hob and appliances can go, given drainage and service runs.
You are unsure how much glazing you can have without falling foul of energy rules.
You want to know whether your project needs planning permission or can go ahead under permitted development.
You are worried about how you will manage without a kitchen during the building work and want a design that keeps disruption to a minimum.
context_heading: What to understand about kitchen extension architects
context: In the UK, the title 'architect' is protected by law, so only people on the Architects Registration Board (ARB) register can call themselves architects. They must follow the ARB code of conduct and hold professional indemnity insurance. Many practices are also RIBA Chartered Practices, but architectural designers and technologists can also do excellent work, so it is worth knowing which type of professional you are hiring.

Before you appoint anyone, check the ARB register and ask for a written appointment that sets out the services, fees and responsibilities. Building regulations approval, planning permission and party wall matters are separate processes that your architect can help you navigate, but they are not handled by iComply.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Describe the current layout of your home and what you want the new kitchen extension to include.
Mention whether you already have drawings or a clear idea of the size and shape you are after.
Say whether you have any constraints such as a limited budget, a tight timescale or a need to stay in the house during works.
Explain any planning history you know of, such as previous extensions or listed building status.
Note whether you need help with planning permission and building regulations or just design work.
Include your postcode so we can introduce you to a professional who works in your area.
questions: Are you on the Architects Registration Board register?
How will you approach the kitchen layout to make the most of light and space?
What experience do you have with kitchen extensions that involve moving drainage and services?
Will you handle planning permission and building regulations applications on my behalf?
How do you charge for your work, and what is included in your fee?
Can you provide a written appointment that sets out your services and responsibilities?

faqs.q: Do I need an architect for a kitchen extension?
faqs.a: Not always, but a registered architect can help you get the most from the space, especially if the layout is complex or you need planning permission. Architectural designers and technologists can also do excellent work, so it is worth checking which type of professional you are hiring.

faqs.q: How do I check if someone is a registered architect?
faqs.a: You can check the Architects Registration Board (ARB) register online. Only people on that register can legally call themselves architects in the UK.

faqs.q: Will my kitchen extension need planning permission?
faqs.a: Some extensions can be built under permitted development, but others need planning permission. Your architect can advise you on this and help you prepare an application if needed.

faqs.q: What should I have ready before I contact an architect?
faqs.a: It helps to have a clear idea of what you want, any measurements or photos of the existing space, and a rough budget in mind. The more detail you can give, the better the professional can respond.

extra_heading: Choosing between local kitchen extension architects
extra: Searching for a kitchen extension architect near me usually means you want someone who can visit your home, see how the light falls and understand the quirks of your existing kitchen before putting pencil to paper. Local knowledge matters here, because how your extension sits with neighbouring properties and the street scene can shape what planning allows. It is worth asking each practice how familiar they are with your local planning authority and how often they work on homes like yours.

When you compare the practices we introduce you to, look beyond the headline fee and ask what the appointment actually covers. Some architects price design work separately from planning and building regulations applications, and some include site visits during the build, so a written breakdown helps you compare like with like. Ask how they will handle the kitchen layout itself, since drainage, service runs and glazing often drive the cost of an extension more than the shape of the walls.

At a first appointment, expect to walk through your existing kitchen and garden together and talk about how you want to use the new space day to day. A good conversation will cover where you cook, where you gather, how much glazing you hope for and how you might manage without a working kitchen during the works. Come away with a clear sense of the next steps, what information they need from you and how their fees are structured, so you can weigh up your options calmly.

extra_faqs.q: Should the architect also design the kitchen itself?
extra_faqs.a: Some architects will plan the kitchen layout as part of the extension design, while others leave the cabinetry and appliances to a kitchen specialist. It is worth agreeing early who is responsible for the layout, service positions and finishes so nothing falls between the two.

extra_faqs.q: How local does a kitchen extension architect need to be?
extra_faqs.a: There is no rule, but someone who can reach your home easily is better placed to visit during design and construction, and may already know your local planning authority's approach. Ask how many site visits their appointment includes and whether travel is charged.

extra_faqs.q: Can I stay in my home while the extension is built?
extra_faqs.a: Many people do, but losing the kitchen for a stretch is the hardest part. Talk to your architect about a temporary cooking arrangement and a design that phases the work sensibly, so you can plan around the disruption.
